title: Juvenile & B.G. Talk Cash Money & No Limit Tour, New Orleans Rap History & ‘Ha’ Music Video
summary: The two Cash Money mainstays plan on releasing new music together soon.
contentText:
The Cash Money & No Limit Tour kicks off today, and we had Juvenile and B.G. stop by the Billboard offices in New York City recently to talk about how this New Orleans rap dream tour came about.

By the time Juvenile shook up the game with the song and music video for “Ha,” B.G.’s sophomore album Chopper City was already considered a classic in New Orleans and surrounding areas. However, here up north, seeing that video was the first time we had ever heard of this particular version of Cash Money (see: New Jack City .) My friends and I were mesmerized by the raw cinematography we watched as we were hearing this dude from down south asking us question after question. There was something about Juvie’s delivery that was different from anything else in the game at that particular moment in time.

Cash Money took rap by storm after that music video hit MTV and BET. All of a sudden, we were rockin’ crisp white tees and Girbaud jeans over our white on white Nike Air Force 1s, and incorporating “bling” into our lexicon, which was funny because there was another New Orleans clique on scene in No Limit who were also churning out hit sin their own right. This is why you really can’t listen to people that say most of the New York City area had some type of bias when it came to Southern rap. Cash Money, No Limit, and Rap-A-Lot were getting plenty of play in the North Jersey neighborhood I grew up in.

Both B.G. and Juvie have a natural chemistry that’s apparent in the interview you’re about to read. They’ve been friends and collaborators going on three decades now and continue to work on new music together. They’ve floated the idea of a collab album and have a bunch of stuff already in the bank, but first they want to get out something that will also feature another fellow Louisiana native.

“We were supposed to do the Magnolia Landlords with me, him and Boosie , but I got caught up and I don’t like to put anything out,” Juvenile said after I asked if they have anything in the works. B.G. then added that they’ve been busy in the studio and that his legal issues are finally behind him. “We sitting on a gang of records. I’m talking about crack rock too,” he said. “The legal stuff behind me. I ain’t on paper no more. I’m a free man, so I can do what I want when I want. I can be Gizzle.”

Check out our conversation below.

Let’s talk about this tour. You guys did the Verzuz with No Limit, and now you’re going on tour with them. Was the response to the Verzuz the catalyst for the tour?

Juvenile: Definitely. I mean, when we was doing it, we were saying this probably could turn into something else if it goes great. But the fact that we’re able to go out and and do the Verzuz and do a tour, I think that’s something that we should all behold too. That’s a blessing right there.

B.G. how’s that been for you? You came home, moved to Vegas, you just dropped an album. You got right back into the mix, man.

B.G.: To do 12 and a half years and come back and have another shot at it — it’s a real blessing. People don’t do as much time as I did and remain relevant in this game. To be snatched off the streets in my prime, and do 12 years and come home and people still want to hear from you, still have a fanbase that truly f—k you, lets you know that you made timeless music and connected with the people in a way that’s just priceless, you know what I mean? And then not to mention, I got brothers that are legends that remained relevant the whole time that I was gone — so it was kind of easy for me to come back and get off into it and piggyback off what they already was doing. Still holding it down and representing.

Were you were you like when you performed now like the first time you performed after coming home and all that were you like nervous?

B.G.: My first show was the Essence Festival. When I came home, they had tried to violate me.

For lyrics and all that stuff, right? As if you were a mob boss.

B.G.: Man, they was on my trail, man. But I fought it, and I went to court and the judge ruled in my favor, and I was able to get back into it. And the timing just was so perfect, because once they gave me permission to rap again, it was right before Essence Fest.

That’s home, so you felt comfortable.

B.G.: Yeah, yeah, and the first concert was at Essence was sold out, like 40,000-plus. I was really excited. That was the moment that I had been waiting for. To get back on stage after all that time and see what the response was gonna be like? Man, it was incredible.

I’m from the East Coast, right? North Jersey to be exact. And I’ve always wanted to ask, and I’m sure you guys probably have talked about this before, but the rise of Cash Money and No Limit kind of happened at the same time. So, was there like a rivalry in the city? Was it a friendly one? Was it more of a personal thing? Was there some things for you guys to get over to be able to make the Verzuz and tour happen 20-30 years later?

J: I would say a little bit of both, because a lot of the cats in No Limit, we friends with them, right? So, it ain’t really no rivalry to the point where we try to hurt each other on some beef stuff. But do you want to do better and outdo… really, not just them, we was competitive against everybody to be honest. We were trying to outdo everybody.

B.G.: Nah, facts.

J: I think it was more like checking to see how many records they sold first week versus what we did. Stuff like that. There was always a little bit something there, but not nothing major like that.

B.G.: Back then it was a lot of street politics involved too, right? Because we was representing the Magnolia and the 13 and this side uptown, and they was representing the Callio. It was our entourages that basically had beef. Mac, Fiend, them were our homies for real. And then our CEOs really was, you know, ego trippin’. Like he said, it was a competitive thing, man — because I think they got they deal before we got our deal, right? We was looking at what they was doing.

J: Definitely watching what they were doing.

B.G.: And once we got our shot and our whole thing was good, now it’s our turn to put on for the city.

You guys were already poppin’ in New Orleans when Master P and No Limit got their deals, right? You were selling a bunch of records.

J: We pretty much had New Orleans. We were poppin’ in New Orleans a little bit before the whole No Limit thing took off.

B.G.: Absolutely.

J: They got the deal before us. But as for as being poppin’ in New Orleans? It wasn’t just there. We had the whole Southern region.

Like how? Selling mixtapes?

B.G.: Nah, albums. We were dropping full albums.

J: We were the only ones who didn’t put singles out, because we would make you go buy our whole album.

So, how were people able to get those albums?

B.G.: They was going to stores.

You guys were were taking the stock and going to record stores door to door?

J: We had distributor named Southwest [who] distributed throughout the South. So, every week we would load up.

B.G.: We had U-Haul trucks [ Laughs .]

J: We would bring the boxes to to him, and he would distribute. We was getting around because of that. We had a larger range than the average label.

Word, okay. Because back in the day motherf—kers tell stories about how they had a trunk full of CDs and tapes.

B.G.: I mean, we played that game too, right?

J: I actually did that.

Early on, right?

J: That was before I was with Cash Money. I was in the trunk for real.

Do you remember what album you were selling?

J: Oh, it wasn’t an album. It was “Bounce (For the Juvenile).” That was one long song. Back in the days, we would go to the club and record right there live. So, I had a little live…
